summary:
Mayotte is a French overseas department in the Indian Ocean and stands under the French national framework. The national rules on identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination, marriage and custody place extend to the island, including its places of deprivation of liberty.

Trans detainees in French prisons are held according to the gender shown on their identity document under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them; placement follows the document marker rather than anatomy. This framework binds Mayotte's establishments as French law.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. The opinion extends to local jails as French establishments.

Legal gender change without surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatric certificates or proof of medical intervention was approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017; a court appearance is still required to change the gender marker, while a first-name change can be done at the registry office. The National Assembly also voted the simplification of legal gender change. French law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity: article 225-1 of the Penal Code was amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that account. Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023, after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the written law is not the whole of what a couple faces. Same-sex marriage has been legal here since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law, as available.

A 16 May 2020 French report recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, with around 1,870 victims identified by police compared with around 1,380 in 2018; the figure is national and covers homophobic and transphobic incidents together, not Mayotte alone.

Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report critical of youth gender-affirming care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the government, with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first national youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2.
tangentialFactors:
Conversion therapy was banned by Senate vote on 7 December 2020, National Assembly concurrence on 25 January 2022 and publication on 1 February 2022, with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and a 30,000 euro fine.

Transgender people are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces. In March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms.

The National Academy of Medicine has characterised increased demand for gender care as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution, without changing actual practice. France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, though transgender rights organisations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery performed in-country was legalised in 1979 after previously only being accessible abroad.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been banned since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of services and goods. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euros fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage was approved by the National Assembly on 12 February 2013 by 329-229, by the Senate on 12 April with amendments accepted 23 April, ruled constitutional 17 May 2013, signed 18 May 2013 and published the next day, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) have been available since 1999. Same-sex sexual activity in private was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791; a discriminatory age of consent under Vichy article 334, moved to article 331 on 8 February 1945 setting 21 years for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual, was lowered to 18 in 1974 and repealed 4 August 1982 to equalise at 15. A 1960 Mirguet amendment doubling the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity was repealed in 1980; in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, with Senate vote still pending. The 20 June 1983 ban on men who have sex with men donating blood was replaced by one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016, four-month abstinence from 2 April 2020, and removal of deferral on 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation.

Of 27 overseas deputies, 11 voted for same-sex marriage and 11 against, with 1 abstaining and 3 absent.

Residents of Mayotte seeking to change their legal gender marker must go before a court, though a first-name change can be done at the registry office; the simplified procedure approved in 2016 and effective 1 January 2017 removed the requirement for surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatric certificates or proof of medical intervention.

The Labour Code protects residents against exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and against sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity, and article 225-1 of the Penal Code covers gender identity discrimination since 18 November 2016. Transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison since 2017.

Transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery performed in-country has been legal since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found healthcare provision suffers lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location.

Residents held in custody are placed according to their identity-document gender under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities. The CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons.

No LGBT-friendly lawyer is referenced in Mayotte in the directory covering Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and other towns; a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law, is listed as available.

In March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 16 May 2020 report recording a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, with around 1,870 victims identified by police compared with around 1,380 in 2018, is a national French figure covering homophobic and transphobic incidents together; no Mayotte-specific breakdown is sourced here, and no trans-specific violence figure for Mayotte is documented in this inventory.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 is national in scope and does not identify Mayotte establishments by name; its application to local jails follows from Mayotte standing under the French framework rather than from a documented Mayotte inspection.

The status of the legislation to ban medical transition under age 18, which passed the Senate in May 2024 and was opposed by the government, is unresolved as of the last sourced update on 23 July 2024.

Whether the directory's absence of a referenced LGBT-friendly lawyer in Mayotte reflects an absence of willing counsel or only of directory coverage is not sourced.
